claims.claim: The WHO working definition: patient safety is the absence of preventable harm to a patient during health care, with the risk of unnecessary harm reduced to an acceptable minimum; WHO calls 'first, do no harm' the most fundamental principle of any health care service.

Patient safety is also described as a framework of organized activities — cultures, processes, procedures, behaviours, technologies, and environments — that lower risks, reduce avoidable harm, make error less likely, and lessen harm's impact when it does occur.
Around 1 in 10 patients is harmed while receiving health care, and more than half of that harm is considered preventable.

The modern patient-safety movement began with the 1999 Institute of Medicine report To Err Is Human, which estimated that 44,000-98,000 Americans died each year as a result of preventable harm; AHRQ's PSNet notes the exact number of deaths remains controversial.

An adverse event is patient harm that arises from medical care rather than from the underlying disease; a preventable adverse event results from error or failure to apply an accepted prevention strategy; a near miss exposes a patient to a hazardous situation without causing harm; an error is an act of commission or omission that exposes a patient to risk.

Common sources of avoidable patient harm named by WHO include medication errors, patient falls, health care-associated infections, and unsafe surgical procedures — including wrong-site surgery, which WHO links to failure to correctly identify patients.

Most harmful mistakes result from multiple interacting factors — system and organizational issues (complexity of interventions, workflow disruptions, staffing and resource constraints), technological issues, human factors such as communication breakdowns, ineffective teamwork, fatigue, and cognitive bias, and patient-related factors — rather than from a single careless individual.

The systems approach holds that most errors reflect predictable human failings within poorly designed systems, so safety improves when the underlying system is redesigned to make errors harder and to catch them before they reach the patient; James Reason's Swiss cheese model describes how layers of flawed defences line up to produce harm, and most serious errors are committed by competent, well-intentioned clinicians.

A safety culture is one in which people speak up about concerns, report errors and close calls without fear of blame, and treat incidents as learning opportunities; just culture recognizes that most errors are system-driven while still holding individuals accountable for negligence or deliberate disregard of safety practices.

Core patient-safety practices include correctly identifying patients, checking allergies, cleaning hands at the right moments, and communicating clearly; WHO describes hand hygiene as the single most important measure for preventing germ transmission in health care, and AHRQ's TeamSTEPPS provides evidence-based teamwork tools built around communication, situation monitoring, and mutual support.

Patients are active partners in their own safety: patients can help prevent medical errors by being active members of the care team, asking questions when they have doubts, and telling providers about allergies and all medicines they take; research shows patients who are more involved in their care tend to get better results.

AHRQ is the lead federal agency for patient safety research in the United States, and nursing education treats safety as a core professional competency (the OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing text emphasizes the Quality and Safety Education for Nurses framework).

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many patients die from preventable harm in U.S. hospitals each year?
positions: The 1999 Institute of Medicine report To Err Is Human estimated 44,000-98,000 deaths per year.
Later studies have produced both lower and (more often) higher estimates, and PSNet states the number of deaths that directly result from preventable adverse events is controversial.
WHO currently summarizes the global picture as around 1 in 10 patients harmed, with more than half of harm preventable.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson cites the 1999 estimate as the historical landmark that launched the movement (attributed to the IOM report via the AHRQ PSNet primer) and uses WHO's 'around 1 in 10 patients harmed, more than half preventable' as the current summary. No single death count is presented as exact.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much of patient harm is truly preventable?
positions: WHO states more than 50% of harm is preventable, and up to 80% of harm in primary and ambulatory settings may be avoidable.

PSNet distinguishes preventable adverse events (due to error or failure to apply an accepted prevention strategy) from ameliorable adverse events (not preventable, but could have been less harmful) and events due to negligence.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses WHO's 'more than half preventable' figure and explains preventable-versus-ameliorable as a technical distinction, avoiding any claim that all harm can be eliminated.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft's boilerplate ('Patient Safety is a foundational concept in Nursing & Allied Health Foundations', 'a college-level explanation names the concept', etc.) contains no factual claims; it was discarded wholesale and replaced with source-verified content.
